Most small business websites take one to two weeks to build when the owner sends text and photos on time. Bigger sites with custom features take longer. The real delay is almost never the design. It's waiting on content, logos and approvals. Here's what happens in each week, and what you can do to speed it up.

## What happens before the build starts?

Every project starts with a call. You explain what the business does, who your customers are and what you want a visitor to do. That takes about thirty minutes.

After the call comes a written plan. It lists the pages, the sections and the tone. You read it and say yes or ask for changes. Nothing gets built until you approve it. That plan is the reason the build goes fast. Nobody's guessing.

Now the homework. You need a logo, a handful of real photos, your hours, your phone number and a short list of services. If you have those ready, you've already saved several days. If you don't, this is where projects stall.

## How long does the build itself take?

For a one-page site, the build usually takes a few days. A five-page site takes closer to a week. Mayfly builds with fast static pages, so there's no plugin hunting and no waiting on a page builder to load.

During the build you'll see a private preview link. Open it on your phone first. Most of your customers will see the site on a phone, so that's the view that matters. Speed counts too. Google measures loading and stability with [Core Web Vitals](https://web.dev/articles/vitals), and a slow page loses visitors before they read a word.

Here's a rough timeline for the Business plan, which covers up to five pages:

- Days 1 to 3: discovery call and written plan
- Days 4 to 8: build and first preview
- Days 9 to 12: your feedback and one round of revisions
- Days 13 to 14: launch and a short walkthrough

A Starter site can move faster because there's less to build.

## What slows a website project down?

Almost always, it's content. A site needs real words and real photos, and owners are busy. A missing logo file can cost three days. Even a "let me ask my partner" can cost a week.

The second cause is scope creep. You start with five pages and then add a store, a booking system and a blog. Each of those is a good idea. Each one also moves the date. Extra pages cost $149 each and extra sections cost $49, so it's easy to see what a change adds.

The third cause is silence. Feedback that arrives in two days keeps a project moving. Feedback that arrives in two weeks doesn't. Set a reminder for yourself.

## Should you rush a launch?

No, but you shouldn't drag it out either. A site that goes live in two weeks and improves every month beats a perfect site that launches in six months.

Google says it wants content that helps people, written for people first, and its [helpful content guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) is worth a read before you write your service pages. You don't need thousands of words. You need clear answers to the questions your customers already ask.

Launch with the basics. Add more once real visitors show you what they want. Small text and photo updates are included every month on both plans, so the site can grow without a new project each time.

## What's the fastest way to get your site live?

Do the homework first. Gather your logo, six to ten photos, your hours and a plain list of services. Write two sentences about what makes your business different. Then book the call.

Reply to previews within a day or two. Say what you like and what you'd change, in plain words. You don't need design terms. "The phone number is too small" is perfect feedback.

That's the whole trick. The design is quick. Your speed decides the date.
